[MUJAHID:v1p1/r1] MUJAHID, d. 104 · أصحاب رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Companions report that they learned ten verses at a time from the Prophet and did not move on until they understood their knowledge and practice, learning Quran, knowledge, and action together.

[MUJAHID:v1p158/r3] MUJAHID, d. 104 · الحسن | reports | Al-Hasan interprets touching women here as sexual intercourse.
[MUQATIL:4:43/r1] MUQATIL, d. 150 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet said God had brought forward wine's prohibition; this first restriction followed a drunken Maghrib prayer at ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. ʿAwf's meal, where ʿAlī misrecited 109:1. | mentions 109:1

[MUQATIL:4:43/r12] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | God pardons their earlier drunken prayer and their practice of tayammum without ablution before these rules were prohibited.
[MUQATIL:4:43/r2] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | reports | After this first restriction, they drank only after the dawn prayer until later morning, so they prayed the first prayer sober.
[MUQATIL:4:43/r3] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | reports | An Anṣārī, ʿUthbān b. Mālik, later served Saʿd wine; their fight broke Saʿd's nose, and wine was then prohibited in al-Māʾida after the Confederates campaign.
[MUQATIL:4:43/r4] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The exception for a person passing through refers to a traveler who lacks water.
[MUQATIL:4:43/r5] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | reports | The sickness clause was revealed concerning ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. ʿAwf, who was wounded and in a state of major impurity; washing was difficult and feared to harm him.
[MUQATIL:4:43/r6] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | A wound or illness permits tayammum even when water is available, if washing risks harm.
[MUQATIL:4:43/r7] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | reports | The clause about a healthy traveler was revealed concerning ʿĀʾisha, and the tayammum verse came in her affair between two prayers.
[MUQATIL:4:43/r8] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Coming from al-ghāʾiṭ means coming from the place of relieving oneself; touching women here means sexual intercourse.
[MUQATIL:4:43/r9] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The healthy person without water and the sick person who has water both perform tayammum.

[FARRA:v1p268/r11] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | A person in major ritual impurity may not approach prayer until washing, except while traveling and unable to find water.
[FARRA:v1p268/r12] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | The exception is a traveler unable to find water.
[FARRA:v1p268/r13] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | Tayammum means intending clean earth wherever it may be found.
[FARRA:v1p268/r14] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | Tayammum consists of one strike for the face and one for the hands, for a person in major impurity or otherwise.

[NAHHAS:v1p457/r7] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | Illness means inability to use water or fear of death from cold or wounds; travel means lacking water.
[NAHHAS:v1p457/r8] NAHHAS, d. 338 · بعض الفقهاء | reports | Some jurists say aw here means “and”; skilled grammarians reject that because the listed conditions differ, preferring a shifted word order that makes the clauses fit together.
[NAHHAS:v1p457/r9] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | The proposed word order is “do not approach prayer drunk, or after relieving yourselves or touching women; and if junub and seeking prayer, purify yourselves,” a shift comparable to 20:129. | mentions 20:129
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p124/r5] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · author | holds | The form with alif makes the action mutual between man and woman; Arabic uses the reciprocal pattern in jāmaʿtu al-marʾa, not jamaʿtu.
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p124/r6] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · author | holds | Without alif, the verb is an action by the man alone, as in the wording if you marry believing women. | mentions 4:25
[FARISI-HUJJA:v3p163/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو وعاصم وابن عامر | reports | These readers read lāmastum with alif here and at 5:6. | mentions 5:6
[FARISI-HUJJA:v3p163/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · حمزة والكسائي | reports | Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read lamastum without alif here and in al-Māʾida. | mentions 5:6
[FARISI-HUJJA:v3p163/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Touch can mean hand contact or extend beyond physical contact; Qurʾānic uses of touching heaven and a book show the broader sense, while ‘with their hands’ disambiguates the latter. | mentions 72:8, 6:7
[FARISI-HUJJA:v3p163/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · عمر وعلي | reports | According to ʿUmar and ʿAlī, seclusion can have the legal standing of touch.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v3p163/r5] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · الصحابة | reports | The Companions split between hand contact and intercourse; none combined the meanings, so interpreting both violates their agreement.
[SULAMI:v1p149/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | Intoxication includes wine as well as heedlessness, desire, worldly life, wealth, family, children, sins, and even acts of obedience; all can prevent full prayer and standing apart from other concerns.
[SULAMI:v1p149/r2] SULAMI, d. 412 · الواسطي | reports | The command means not to approach communion with God unless separated from all contingent beings and everything in them.
[THALABI:v3p311#2/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The verse was revealed about Companions who drank wine and came to prayer intoxicated, unable to tell how many units they prayed or what they said.
[THALABI:v3p311#2/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The word means intoxicated with wine; سكارى is the plural of سكران.
[THALABI:v3p311#2/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · إبراهيم النخعي | reports | Al-Nakha'i reads جنبًا as another of the two Arabic forms for the word.
[THALABI:v3p312/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The phrase means knowing and reciting what one says in prayer; after this verse they avoided intoxication at prayer times until wine was prohibited in al-Ma'idah. | mentions 5:90
[THALABI:v3p312/r10] THALABI, d. 427 · علي وابن عباس وابن جبير وابن زيد ومجاهد والحكم والحسن بن مسلم وابن كثير | reports | One group understands the exception as travelers who lack water, allowing them to use dry ablution.
[THALABI:v3p312/r11] THALABI, d. 427 · عبد الله وابن المسيب وابن يسار والضحاك والحسن وعكرمة وإبراهيم وعطاء الخراساني والنخعي والزيدي | reports | Another group takes the exception to mean passing through a mosque without remaining there while in major impurity; here الصلاة means the mosque or prayer place.
[THALABI:v3p312/r12] THALABI, d. 427 · author | reports | Ansar whose doors opened into the mosque became impure and lacked another route to water; the report explains the permission to pass through.
[THALABI:v3p312/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · الضحاك بن مزاحم | reports | Al-Dahhak interprets the drunkenness here as sleepiness, not wine intoxication.
[THALABI:v3p312/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · عائشة | reports | The Prophet said that a person who becomes drowsy in prayer should sleep until alert, lest he seek forgiveness while actually cursing himself.
[THALABI:v3p312/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · عائشة | reports | The Prophet said a sleepy person praying should leave, since he might unknowingly pray against himself.
[THALABI:v3p312/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو هريرة | reports | The Prophet said that if a night worshipper's tongue stumbles over the Qur'an and he does not know what he is saying, he should lie down.
[THALABI:v3p312/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · عبيدة السلماني | reports | Ubayda al-Salmani says the verse includes a person holding back urine; he cites the prohibition on praying while resisting the two impurities.
[THALABI:v3p312/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | جنبًا is accusative as a circumstantial qualifier: do not approach prayer while in a state of major ritual impurity.
[THALABI:v3p312/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · إبراهيم النخعي | reports | Ibrahim al

-Nakha'i reads جنبًا with a quiescent nun.
[THALABI:v3p312/r9] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | جنب is used unchanged for a man, two people, women, and groups; its verb is أجنب يجنب, and janābah is named for distance because the impure person keeps away until purified.
[THALABI:v3p313/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The root sense of عبور is crossing or traversing; one says a person crossed a road or river when passing through it.
[THALABI:v3p313/r10] THALABI, d. 427 · مالك والأوزاعي وأبو يوسف | reports | Malik, al-Awza'i, and Abu Yusuf require dry ablution and prayer in this case, without repeating it later.
[THALABI:v3p313/r11] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو حنيفة | reports | Abu Hanifa says not to use dry ablution or pray in this situation; wait until water is found, perform ablution, and then pray.
[THALABI:v3p313/r12] THALABI, d. 427 · الزهري | reports | Al-Zuhri reads الغيط instead of الغائط.
[THALABI:v3p313/r13] THALABI, d. 427 · مجاهد والحسن والمؤرخ | reports | The related forms الغيط, الغوط, and الغائط denote low ground: Mujahid says a valley, al-Hasan a valley's hollow, and al-Mu'arrikh a concealed low basin surrounded by vines.
[THALABI:v3p313/r14] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Because people relieved themselves in such secluded low places, الغائط became a euphemism for bowel needs; its plural is غيطان, with the verbs غاط يغوط and تغوط يتغوط.
[THALABI:v3p313/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | مرضى is the plural of مريض.
[THALABI:v3p313/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · أم سلمة | reports | A report from Umm Salama says the Prophet declared his mosque forbidden to menstruating women and men in major impurity, except Muhammad and his family: Ali, Fatima, Hasan, and Husayn.
[THALABI:v3p313/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · جماعة من الفقهاء | reports | Jurists allow dry ablution for illnesses harmed by water, including smallpox, wounds, sores, and a fracture covered with splints.
[THALABI:v3p313/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · عطاء والحسن | reports | Ata and al-Hasan deny dry ablution when water is available, citing the verse's condition that water not be found.
[THALABI:v3p313/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · جابر | reports | Jabir recounts that an injured man in a campaign washed after a wet dream despite his companions' advice and died; the Prophet condemned them and prescribed dry ablution, a wound covering, wiping it, and washing the rest.
[THALABI:v3p313/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · author | rejects | The author rejects Ata and al-Hasan's restriction, using the Prophet's instruction to the injured man to show that harmful water may be avoided even when present.
[THALABI:v3p313/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Travel permits dry ablution when water is lacking, whether the journey is long or short.
[THALABI:v3p313/r9] THALABI, d. 427 · الشافعي ومحمد بن الحسن | reports | If water unexpectedly disappears in a city or village, al-Shafi'i and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan require dry ablution and prayer, followed by repeating the prayer.
[THALABI:v3p314/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · حمزة والكسائي وخلف | reports | Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf read لمستم without the alif here and in al-Ma'idah; Abu Ubayd prefers this reading. | mentions 5:6
[THALABI:v3p314/r10] THALABI, d. 427 · ابن عباس والحسن البصري ومحمد بن الحسين | reports | A group, including Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan al-Basri, and Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, holds that touching never invalidates ablution.
[THALABI:v3p314/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · الباقون وأبو حاتم | reports | The remaining readers retain the alif in both places, the reading preferred by Abu Hatim. | mentions 5:6
[THALABI:v3p314/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · ابن عباس والحسن ومجاهد وقتادة | reports | Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, and Qatada interpret touching women as sexual intercourse.
[THALABI:v3p314/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas tells Sa'id ibn Jubayr that the Arabs' interpretation prevailed: touch, contact, and direct intimacy are euphemisms for intercourse, since touch leads to it; he compares cloud and rain both being called sky, as in the cited verse.
[THALABI:v3p314/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · ابن مسعود وابن عمر وأبو عبيدة ومنصور وعبيدة والشعبي والنخعي وحماد والحكم | reports | Another group interprets touching as contact between the two skins, whether or not intercourse occurs.
[THALABI:v3p314/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · الشافعي وابن مسعود وابن عمر والزهري وربيعة | reports | Al-Shafi'i and the listed authorities hold that a man's touching any part of a woman's body, by hand or otherwise, invalidates ablution.
[THALABI:v3p314/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · الأوزاعي | reports | Al-Awza'i says touching with the hand invalidates ablution, but contact with another part of the body does not, by analogy with touching the genitals.
[THALABI:v3p314/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · مالك والليث بن سعد وأحمد بن حنبل وإسحاق بن راهويه | reports | Malik, al-Layth, Ahmad, and Ishaq say lustful touching invalidates ablution, while touch without desire does not.
[THALABI:v3p314/r9] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو حنيفة وأبو يوسف | reports | Abu Hanifa and Abu Yusuf require an obscene, desire-arousing contact for ablution to be invalidated.
[THALABI:v3p315/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · الثوري | reports | Al-Thawri has two reports: one follows the view that touch does not invalidate ablution, while the other follows Malik's view that touch of the hand does.
[THALABI:v3p315/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shafi'i argues that لمس most often means hand contact, citing the Prophetic prohibition on mulamasa sales and a poem using لمس for touching with the palm.
[THALABI:v3p315/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · أبيه | reports | A report says he touched her with his hand, supporting the hand-contact sense of mulamasa.
[THALABI:v3p315/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · معاذ | reports | Muadh reports that when a man asked about enjoying an unrelated woman short of intercourse, the Prophet instructed him to perform a thorough ablution.
[THALABI:v3p315/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · عائشة | reports | Aisha says she slept in front of the Prophet with her feet toward his prayer direction; when he prostrated he nudged her feet, and she folded them.
[THALABI:v3p315/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · عائشة | reports | Aisha says that while she lay across before the Prophet as he prayed, he touched her foot when he wanted to perform the witr prayer.
[THALABI:v3p315/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · عائشة | reports | Aisha recounts finding the Prophet prostrating and invoking God's refuge; some reports add that he asked whether her devil had come, after her hand touched his foot during prayer.
[THALABI:v3p315/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | These reports explain why the jurists who count touch as invalidating ablution limit that rule to contact with desire.
[THALABI:v3p315/r9] THALABI, d. 427 · عائشة | reports | Aisha reports that the Prophet kissed one of his wives and then prayed without performing ablution.
[THALABI:v3p316/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · الشافعي | reports | In al-Shafi'i's school, intentional direct touching of a young adult woman, living or dead, invalidates ablution.
[THALABI:v3p316/r10] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Dry ablution is a distinctive privilege of this Muslim community.
[THALABI:v3p316/r11] THALABI, d. 427 · حذيفة | reports | Hudhayfa reports the Prophet saying that this community was favored with angel-like prayer rows, the earth as a mosque, and its soil as purification when water is lacking.
[THALABI:v3p316/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · الشافعي | reports | In al-Shafi'i's school, touching hair, teeth, or nails does not invalidate ablution.
[THALABI:v3p316/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shafi'i has two views on touching a little girl, an older woman, or an unmarriageable female relative: it invalidates because intentional, or does not because desire is absent.
[THALABI:v3p316/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو قتادة | reports | Abu Qatada reports that the Prophet prayed while carrying Umama, daughter of Zaynab; he set her down when prostrating and lifted her when standing.
[THALABI:v3p316/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · الجمهور | reports | The majority say that touch invalidates ablution regardless of whether a barrier is thick or thin.
[THALABI:v3p316/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · مالك | reports | Malik says contact through a thin barrier invalidates ablution, but contact through a thick barrier does not.
[THALABI:v3p316/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · الليث وربيعة | reports | Al-Layth and Rabi'a say contact invalidates ablution whether the barrier is thick or thin.
[THALABI:v3p316/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The author argues that contact through a barrier does not invalidate ablution: the verse names touching the woman, whereas with a barrier one touches the barrier; an oath not to touch her likewise remains unbroken.
[THALABI:v3p316/r9] THALABI, d. 427 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shafi'i has two views on whether the person touched loses ablution: yes, because both share in pleasure; or no, as in Aisha's report of touching the Prophet's foot.
[THALABI:v3p317/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · عائشة | reports | Aisha recounts losing a borrowed necklace at al-Abwa' or al-Bayda/Dhat al-Jaysh; the party lacked water and was in ritual impurity, so the dry-ablution verse was revealed. Her camel was later moved and the necklace found beneath it; Usayd called it one of the family's blessings.
[THALABI:v3p317/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · علي وابن عباس وابن حمزة ومالك والشافعي والليث بن سعد وأحمد بن حنبل | reports | One position requires prayer time to enter before dry ablution, though one ablution may cover two obligatory prayers; its proponents treat it as emergency purification like that of a woman with irregular bleeding.
[THALABI:v3p317/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · author | reports | The proponents cite the Prophet's instruction to perform dry ablution and pray wherever the prayer time catches a person.
[THALABI:v3p317/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · علي | reports | Ali is reported to have said: perform dry ablution for each prayer.
[THALABI:v3p317/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · عمرو بن قيس | reports | Amr ibn Qays says one should renew dry ablution for every prayer even without an interven

ing ritual impurity.
[THALABI:v3p318/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · سعيد بن المسيب والحسن والثوري وأبو عبيدة | reports | Another group treats dry ablution like water purification: it may precede prayer time and may serve multiple obligatory and voluntary prayers, even after major impurity.
[THALABI:v3p318/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · author | reports | This group cites the Prophet's statement that clean earth is a Muslim's ablution even if water is unavailable for ten years.
[THALABI:v3p318/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The second condition for dry ablution is searching for water: check one's baggage, companions, surrounding directions, high ground, and any approaching person; most jurists invalidate ablution made before searching.
[THALABI:v3p318/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو حنيفة | reports | Abu Hanifa treats searching as recommended rather than required, so dry ablution before searching is valid; he argues that the condition would otherwise apply to voluntary prayer too and that the verse does not require a search.
[THALABI:v3p318/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو حنيفة | reports | Abu Hanifa's analogy: someone told to buy one item and, if unavailable, another is liable if he buys the second before looking for the first.
[THALABI:v3p318/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The third condition is genuine lack of access after searching: thieves, enemies, dangerous animals, fire, risk to life or property, or an inaccessible well all count as lacking water.
[THALABI:v3p318/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The fourth condition is an excuse of illness or travel, as named in the verse.
[THALABI:v3p318/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Illness without harm from water does not permit dry ablution; fear of death does, and a wound feared to be fatal may be avoided with ablution and prayer repeated once the blood can be washed.
[THALABI:v3p319#2/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Any journey qualifying by the name of travel permits the ruling, whether short or long, since God made no distinction.
[THALABI:v3p319#2/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · ابن عمر | reports | Ibn Umar reportedly made dry ablution near Medina after returning from al-Jurf, prayed Asr, entered the city while the sun was still high, and did not repeat the prayer.
[THALABI:v3p319#2/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The fifth condition for dry ablution is an inward intention.
[THALABI:v3p319#2/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The command means to intend clean soil.
[THALABI:v3p319#2/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو حنيفة | reports | Abu Hanifa allows dry ablution on earth and materials of its kind even without particles sticking to the hand, including minerals, plaster, crushed stone, dust, and smooth rock; metal filings are excluded.
[THALABI:v3p319#2/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · مالك | reports | Malik permits dry ablution on earth and what is connected to it, including kinds of soil and trees.
[THALABI:v3p319#2/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · الأوزاعي والثوري | reports | Al-Awza'i and al-Thawri allow dry ablution on earth and anything on it, including trees, stones, clods, ice, and snow.
[THALABI:v3p319#2/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو جهيم | reports | Abu Juhaym reports that the Prophet, after a greeting, wiped his face and hands against a wall before returning the greeting.
[THALABI:v3p319#2/r9] THALABI, d. 427 · الشافعي | prefers | Al-Shafi'i's preferred medium is pure, dusty soil that sticks to the hand: the author says sa'id means soil, tayyib means fertile, and infertile ground is not tayyib; the Prophet's wording singles out soil. | mentions 7:58
[THALABI:v3p319/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو حنيفة | reports | Abu Hanifa allows dry ablution when using water would prolong recovery.
[THALABI:v3p319/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · author | reports | The second view disallows dry ablution for delayed recovery; if only some limbs are injured, wash the safe parts and use dry ablution for the injured, without relying on either alone. Abu Hanifa instead rules by whether most of the body is sound or injured.
[THALABI:v3p319/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The author states that water cannot be used on some limbs while dry ablution is used for others, then presents the Shafi'i disagreement over what to do with an insufficient amount of water.
[THALABI:v3p319/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · الشافعي وأبو حنيفة ومالك والمزني | reports | One Shafi'i view, also held by Abu Hanifa, Malik, and al-Muzani, drops the duty to use insufficient water and accepts dry ablution alone.
[THALABI:v3p319/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · الشافعي | reports | The other Shafi'i view requires using whatever water is available, then completing dry ablution: for major impurity wash any part first; for minor impurity wash in order and use dry ablution for the remaining parts.
[THALABI:v3p319/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | A splint should cover only the fracture and be applied after ritual purification; while the excuse remains one may wipe over it as over leather socks.
[THALABI:v3p319/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · المزني | prefers | Jurists differ over repeating prayers performed while wiping over splints; al-Muzani chooses that no repetition is required.
[THALABI:v3p319/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · علي | reports | A report through Zayd ibn Ali, his father, and grandfather says Hazm broke a forearm and the Prophet ordered him to wipe over the splints; al-Shafi'i says he would accept it if authentic but remains uncertain.
[THALABI:v3p319/r9] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | If a splint was applied without purification or extends beyond the fracture, remove it if safe; if removal risks injury, wash what is possible and repeat the prayer when removal becomes safe.
[THALABI:v3p320/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · الزهري | reports | Al-Zuhri holds that tayammum wipes the face and hands up to the armpits and shoulders, citing a report about the Prophet's journey and Aisha's lost necklace.
[THALABI:v3p320/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Ammar reports that on a journey the tayammum verse was revealed; they struck earth without taking up dust and wiped faces, hands to shoulders, then hand interiors to armpits.
[THALABI:v3p320/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · ابن سيرين، عبد الله بن عمر، جابر بن عبد الله، الحسن البصري، الشعبي، أبو حنيفة، وحنبل، ومالك، والليث | reports | They hold that tayammum takes three strikes: one for the face, one for the hands, and one for the elbows.
[THALABI:v3p320/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A report from Abu al-Samma says the Prophet performed tayammum and wiped his face and forearms, supporting the broader hand extent.
[THALABI:v3p320/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Abu Umama and Ibn Umar report the Prophet's instruction that tayammum is two strikes, for the face and hands to the elbows.
[THALABI:v3p320/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Asla reports that when he was junub the Prophet said the available earth sufficed, then demonstrated striking twice and wiping the arms on both sides.
[THALABI:v3p320/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · علي | reports | Ali says tayammum is two strikes: one for the face and one for the palms.
[THALABI:v3p320/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · سعيد بن المسيب، والأوزاعي، وأحمد، وإسحاق | reports | They hold that one strike suffices for the face and palms, arguing that unqualified hands mean the palm through the wrist, as in the thief's hand-cutting rule. | mentions 5:38
[THALABI:v3p320/r9] THALABI, d. 427 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The one-strike view cites Ammar's report that the Prophet said one strike for the face and palms and that tayammum for major impurity is like tayammum for minor impurity.
[THALABI:v3p321/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The author says a junub person without water performs tayammum like someone in minor impurity; the only contrary report is from Umar and Ibn Masud, who forbid it and say to wait for water and wash.

[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p57/r15] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · الشاعرة | reports | A woman's poem describes a swift camel crossing the wilderness at midday, illustrating traversing in عابري سبيل.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p57/r16] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · علي بن أبي طالب وابن عباس وابن جبير ومجاهد والحكم وغيرهم | reports | They take the wayfarer to be a traveler: one may not approach prayer while junub until bathing, except a traveler may use tayammum.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p57/r17] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · ابن عباس وابن مسعود وعكرمة والنخعي وغيرهم | reports | They take عابر السبيل to mean someone passing through a mosque; this depends on understanding الصلاة as the mosque and prayer place.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p57/r18] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · بعضهم | reports | One reported occasion says some Anṣār had home doors opening into the mosque, so when junub they needed to cross it.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p57/r19] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · الجمهور | reports | Most commentators say the later tayammum clause was revealed when Companions lacked water during the Muraysīʿ expedition while searching for ʿĀʾisha's necklace.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p57/r2] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · عثمان بن عفان وغيره | reports | Uthmān and others held that a drunk person's divorce does not take effect, since the verse shows the intoxicated person does not know what he says.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p57/r20] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · النخعي | reports | Al-Nakhaʿī says the verse was revealed for wounded people who became junub and told the Prophet about their situation.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p57/r21] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · النقاش | reports | Al-Naqqāsh says the verse was revealed concerning ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p57/r3] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | When a man confessed to adultery, the Prophet asked whether he was intoxicated; Ibn ʿAṭiyya infers an intoxicated confession would not bind him.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p57/r4] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Human claims such as divorce, financial admission, or slander affect others' rights, so a drunk person's claim not to know is suspect; adultery confession concerns God's right, so after sobering a claimed lack of awareness is accepted.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p57/r5] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | All criminal penalties remain binding on the intoxicated person.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p57/r6] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | أنتم سكارى is a subject-and-predicate clause functioning circumstantially.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p57/r7] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · ابن فورك | rejects | Ibn Fūrak says the verse prohibits drinking itself so people will not approach prayer intoxicated; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says this is not the apparent meaning.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p57/r8] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · الصحابة | reports | A report says that after this verse the Companions continued drinking but timed or limited it around dawn and evening prayer so no prayer found them intoxicated.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p57/r9] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | ولا جنبا coordinates with the syntactic position of the preceding clause, which is accusative.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p58#2/r1] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | prefers | Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls al-Shāfiʿī's rule for searching for water a good view.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p58#2/r10] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · عمر وعبد الله بن مسعود وغيرهما | reports | A group reported from ʿUmar and Ibn Masʿūd restricts the word to hand contact and says a junub person must bathe or wait for water.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p58#2/r11] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · أبو حنيفة | reports | Abū Ḥanīfa restricts the word to intercourse; touching is not a ritual impurity and a pleasurable kiss does not invalidate ablution.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p58#2/r12] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · مالك | holds | Mālik rules that touching invalidates ablution when done for pleasure, but not without that intent or when the woman touched is one's daughter or mother.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p58#2/r13] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shāfiʿī applies النساء generally: touching one's mother or daughter in any manner invalidates ablution.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p58#2/r14] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Lack of water applies to sick people and travelers; a healthy resident may also qualify when prices are universally exorbitant.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p58#2/r15] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · الحسن | rejects | Al-Ḥasan says one must buy water at any cost, even spending all one's money and becoming destitute; Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects this as inconsistent with ease and absence of hardship (2:185; 22:78). | mentions 2:185, 22:78
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p58#2/r16] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · طائفة | reports | One group requires purchase unless the cost exceeds the usual price by a third or more.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p58#2/r17] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · طائفة | reports | Another group requires paying two or three dirhams for water ordinarily worth one; Ibn ʿAṭiyya places these views within the Mālikī school.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p58#2/r18] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · أشهب | reports | Asked whether one must buy a water-skin for ten dirhams, Ashhab says he does not think this is required of people.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p58#2/r2] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Al-ghāʾiṭ originally meant low ground where Arabs went to relieve themselves; frequent use made it a conventional euphemism.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p58#2/r3] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · قتادة والزهري | reports | Qatāda and al-Zuhrī read من الغيط with a silent yāʾ and no alif; Ibn Jinnī derives it from فيعل and says the medial radical was originally wāw.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p58#2/r4] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · مالك | prefers | Mālik's preferred classification recognizes three kinds of minor impurity: customary output from the passages, loss of reason, and touching.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p58#2/r5] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · أبو حنيفة | reports | Abū Ḥanīfa counts any impurity leaving the body, regardless of where it exits, and does not count touching.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p58#2/r6] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shāfiʿī counts anything leaving either of the two passages, whether customary or not.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p58#2/r7] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Nine kinds unanimously invalidate minor ablution: urine, semen, wadi, madhy, menstrual blood, wind and feces, and loss of reason through insanity, fainting, or deep sleep; other cases remain disputed.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p58#2/r8] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو وابن عامر وعاصم وحمزة والكسائي | reports | Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir, and ʿĀṣim read لامستم; Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read لمستم. The word can mean intercourse, hand contact, or kissing.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p58#2/r9] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · مالك | holds | Mālik gives the wording full scope: intercourse and hand-touching both require tayammum because touching invalidates ablution.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p58/r1] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The sick person intended here is a resident. Tayammum is unanimously permitted for someone who fears death from cold water or illness, apart from a report from ʿAṭāʾ that he must purify even if he dies.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p58/r10] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · إسحق بن راهويه | reports | Isḥāq ibn Rāhwayh says a traveler need search only ahead and nearby.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p58/r11] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · فرقة | reports | Another group requires searching out to about two bowshots or similar.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p58/r12] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · مالك | reports | In the Mālikī school, one walks three miles while looking for water.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p58/r13] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · الشافعي | prefers | Al-Shāfiʿī requires searching without risking loss of companions or prayer time; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls this a good view.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p58/r2] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Within the Mālikī school, as far as Ibn ʿAṭiyya recalls, tayammum is also allowed for someone fearing a new or worsening illness or delayed recovery.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p58/r3] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | A sick person may lack access to water because no one can bring it, or because of the health risks described.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p58/r4] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · داود | rejects | Dāwūd permits tayammum for anyone called sick; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says scholars restrict it to serious conditions such as smallpox, measles, and illnesses endangered by water.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p58/r5] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · مالك وجمهور الفقهاء | holds | Travel here means being away from settled habitation, whether or

[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p59/r1] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | prefers | When obtaining water requires purchase, the duty depends on the buyer’s means and need; he should buy it unless its high price causes harm.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p59/r10] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | In religious usage, tayammum became the established name for the known act of worship.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p59/r11] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · الخليل وغيره | reports | Al-Khalil and others explain ṣaʿīd as the face or surface of the earth; Dhu al-Rumma’s verse supplies poetic evidence for the term.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p59/r12] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · مالك | reports | Malik permits tayammum on any part of the earth—soil, sand, stones, minerals, or saline ground—understanding ṭayyib as pure.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p59/r13] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · طائفة | reports | One group reads ṭayyib as meaning lawful, a sense Ibn ʿAtiyya considers awkward in this context.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p59/r14] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · الشافعي وطائفة | reports | Al-Shafiʿi and a group understand ṭayyib as growth-producing, like 7:58, so ṣaʿīd means soil and tayammum is not allowed on other materials. | mentions 7:58
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p59/r15] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The agreed valid case is tayammum on pure, fertile soil that has not been moved or usurped.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p59/r2] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · مالك وابن نافع | reports | For a healthy resident restrained from accessing water, they say he neither prays nor makes up the prayer.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p59/r3] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · ابن القاسم | reports | For a healthy resident restrained from water, Ibn al-Qasim says to pray and repeat the prayer.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p59/r4] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · أشهب | reports | For a healthy resident restrained from water, Ashhab says to pray without repeating.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p59/r5] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · أصبغ | reports | Asbagh says the restrained resident does not pray but makes it up if using water would make him miss the prayer time.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p59/r6] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · مالك | reports | Malik has two positions in the Mudawwana: perform tayammum without repeating, or repeat; in other works he says to obtain water and wash even after sunrise.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p59/r7] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · طائفة | reports | If a person tayammums with enough time left for ablution and one rakʿa, some say he must repeat and others say he need not.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p59/r8] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Tayammum in Arabic means to intend or head toward something; Ibn ʿAtiyya supports the sense with verses by Imruʾ al-Qays and al-Aʿshā.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p59/r9] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The verb’s sense of intending is also shown by al-Aʿshā of Thaʿlaba’s line about heading toward Qays.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p60#2/r1] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · الجمهور | reports | The majority follows the Qurʾanic order by wiping the face before the hands; some routes of ʿAmmar’s hadith in al-Bukhari put the hands first, as do scholars reasoning by analogy with reversing ablution order.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p60#2/r10] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · مالك | reports | Malik’s Mudawwana requires wiping to the elbows; stopping at the wrists requires repeating within the time, while Ibn Nafiʿ says to repeat ever after.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p60#2/r11] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · مكحول وجماعة من العلماء | reports | Some Maliki jurists require wiping only to the wrists; outside the school, some require only the palms, following ʿAmmar’s hadith and al-Shaʿbi’s position.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p60#2/r12] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · أبو بكر الصديق | reports | Al-Tabari relates that Abu Bakr told ʿAʾisha the tayammum dispensation was a blessing, and that they struck once for the face and once for hands up to shoulders or armpits.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p60#2/r2] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · الجمهور | reports | The majority requires wiping the whole face within its known ablution boundaries, carefully ensuring no part is left untouched.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p60#2/r3] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · محمد بن مسلمة | reports | Some permit leaving hard-to-reach folds and the spaces between fingers unwiped, by analogy with folds in leather socks; this is Muhammad ibn Maslama’s Maliki position.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p60#2/r4] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · مالك | reports | Malik’s Mudawwana prescribes two strikes for tayammum; Ibn al-Jahm says one, and Malik elsewhere says one suffices.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p60#2/r5] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · غيره في المذهب | reports | Some Maliki jurists require repeating tayammum within the prayer time after using one strike, while Ibn Nafiʿ requires repeating it ever after.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p60#2/r6] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · مالك | reports | Malik’s Mudawwana describes wiping left fingertips over the right fingers and up to the elbow, then the inner forearm to the wrist, and repeating on the other arm.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p60#2/r7] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · ابن حبيب | reports | Ibn Habib says the palms should then be wiped against each other; al-Lakhmi interprets the Mudawwana as requiring this, making Ibn Habib’s statement explanatory rather than contradictory.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p60#2/r8] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · طائفة | reports | One group begins with the left hand, reaches the wrist, continues across that palm, and then repeats on the right, to avoid returning to a limb after moving on.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p60#2/r9] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · طائفة | reports | Another group handles soil in the same manner as water, applying it by a wiping motion but without a prescribed sequence of rank.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p60/r1] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Jurists agree tayammum is forbidden on pure gold, silver, precious stones, food, and impure substances.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p60/r10] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · جمهور المذهب | reports | Most Maliki jurists forbid tayammum on wood, while the Mukhtaṣar of al-Waqqar allows it; the school also differs about plants.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p60/r11] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · الطبري | reports | Al-Tabari records four explanations of ṣaʿīd: smooth land, level land, soil, or the face of the earth.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p60/r2] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · مالك | reports | Malik allows tayammum on minerals, while al-Shafiʿi forbids it; al-Lakhmi notes disagreement within the Maliki school as well.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p60/r3] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · أهل المذهب | reports | The Maliki school allows tayammum on both mineral salt and solid salt; other views forbid both or allow mineral salt but forbid solid salt.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p60/r4] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · مالك | reports | The Mudawwana allows tayammum with snow, while Malik prohibits it in other works.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p60/r5] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · ابن علية وابن كيسان | reports | Al-Naqqash reports that Ibn ʿUlayya and Ibn Kaysan allowed tayammum with musk and saffron; Ibn ʿAtiyya rejects this as wholly erroneous.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p60/r6] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | rejects | Ibn ʿAtiyya calls the permission to use musk and saffron for tayammum wholly erroneous.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p60/r7] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · جمهور المذهب | reports | Most Maliki jurists permit tayammum with soil carried in a dish, though some within the school and many outside it prohibit it.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p60/r8] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · أهل المذهب | reports | The school has two positions on tayammum with baked materials such as brick or plaster: permitted or forbidden.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p60/r9] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Jurists disagree over whether tayammum may be performed on a wall.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p61/r1] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · الأعمش | reports | A report from al-Aʿmash says the Prophet wiped to halfway up the forearms; Ibn ʿAtiyya knows of no scholar who followed this report.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p61/r2] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · الداودي | rejects | Al-Dawudi classifies the wrists as obligatory, elbows as sunnah, and armpits as meritorious; Ibn ʿAtiyya says this lacks analogy or evidence.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p61/r3] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · قوم | reports | Some generalize the word “hands” to require wiping from the shoulders.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p61/r4] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · قوم | reports | Others analogize tayammum to ablution and require wiping to the elbows; the majority also extend the wipe to the elbows.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p61/r5] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · قوم | reports | Some stop at the wrists, following the hadith; others analogize purification in tayammum to the legal hand amputation limit.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p61/r6] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · آخرون | reports | Others follow ʿAmmar’s hadith and wipe only the palms.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p61/r7] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · أهل المذهب | reports | The Maliki school differs over whether moving a ring and rubbing between the fingers are obligatory.

[TABRISI:4:43#2/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The clause is circumstantial, governed by taqrabu, with the address pronoun as its subject.

[TABRISI:4:43#2/r6] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | On a journey is accusative by coordination with sick, understood as or while traveling.
[TABRISI:4:43#2/r7] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | After commanding worship in the previous verse, God next mentions prayer as one of the greatest acts of worship.
[TABRISI:4:43#2/r8] TABRISI, d. 548 · ابن عباس وسعيد بن جبير ومجاهد وابن زيد | reports | One interpretation is do not perform prayer while intoxicated.
[TABRISI:4:43#2/r9] TABRISI, d. 548 · عبد الله وسعيد بن المسيب والضحاك وعكرمة والحسن | reports | Another interpretation is do not approach mosques for prayer or otherwise; the exception for passing supports this because crossing is physical movement through a place.
[TABRISI:4:43#3/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The condition means discerning what one says; another explanation is retaining what one recites from the Quran.
[TABRISI:4:43#3/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · علي وابن عباس وسعيد بن جبير ومجاهد | reports | One interpretation forbids prayer in janaba except for travelers, who may pray using tayammum even though it does not remove janaba.
[TABRISI:4:43#3/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · جابر والحسن وعطاء والزهري وإبراهيم | reports | Another interpretation forbids a person in janaba from entering mosques except to pass through; it is also reported from Abu Jaʿfar.
[TABRISI:4:43#3/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | prefers | Al-Tabrisi prefers the mosque-entry interpretation: the ending already gives the junub’s rule when water is unavailable, so reading the opening as prayer would repeat that rule.
[TABRISI:4:43#4/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | One report says the verse was revealed about an ill man from the Ansar who could not rise to perform ablution.

[TABRISI:4:43#4/r12] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The condition covers sick people and travelers: a traveler lacks water, while a sick person may have no one to wash him or fear harm from water.

[TABRISI:4:43#5/r13] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | A drunk person’s contracts, including marriage, sale, and purchase, are invalid; acts that terminate contracts are also ineffective except for the disputed case of divorce.
[TABRISI:4:43#5/r14] TABRISI, d. 548 · أبو حنيفة | reports | Abu Hanifa holds that a drunk person’s divorce takes effect.
[TABRISI:4:43#5/r15] TABRISI, d. 548 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shafiʿi holds in one of his two positions that a drunk person’s divorce does not take effect.
[TABRISI:4:43#5/r16] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | In al-Tabrisi’s school, a drunk person remains liable to all fixed penalties and retaliation, including amputation for theft and punishment for slander or adultery, based on general verses and the school’s consensus.
[TABRISI:4:43#5/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | Another gloss takes ṭayyib as productive soil, contrasted with barren salt land, as in 7:58. | mentions 7:58

[TABRISI:4:43#5/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · عمار بن ياسر ومكحول والطبري | reports | Ammar and Makhul hold for two strikes, one for the face and one for the hands to the wrists; al-Tabari prefers this view.

[TABRISI:4:43#5/r6] TABRISI, d. 548 · سعيد بن المسيب | reports | A report from Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib says one strike suffices when tayammum replaces wudu: wipe the face from hairline to nose tip and hands from wrists to fingertips.
[TABRISI:4:43#5/r7] TABRISI, d. 548 · الزهري | reports | Al-Zuhri reports a third view: wipe to the armpits.
[TABRISI:4:43#5/r8] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | God accepts the concession of tayammum in place of wudu, making the obligation easier.
[TABRISI:4:43#5/r9] TABRISI, d. 548 · قيل | reports | An alternative gloss takes ʿafūw as abundant pardon and forbearance.
[TABRISI:4:43/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · أهل الكوفة غير عاصم | reports | The Kufans except Asim read لمستم without an alif here and in al-Maida.

[TABRISI:4:43/r11] TABRISI, d. 548 · الشاعر | reports | The cited verse’s explanation says talmas means seek.
[TABRISI:4:43/r12] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Tayammum means intending; in law it is the specific act of aiming at the earth and applying soil to designated limbs.

I:4:43/r7] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Junub applies to male or female, singular or plural, describing a person in janaba.
[TABRISI:4:43/r8] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Abir means crossing from one side of a river or road to the other.
[TABRISI:4:43/r9] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Ghait means a low place where people relieved themselves out of sight; its name became a euphemism for the act or result. Another account says it was named for what people discarded there; Murajj defines it as a basin ringed by hills.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p208/r6] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · بعض المفسرين | reports | The Qur'anic list includes ب as a particle that completes the expression; examples include wiping the face, wiping the head, and growing with oil. | mentions 5:6, 23:20
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p88/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · علي بن أبي طالب | reports | In a report from ʿAlī through Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf hosted food and wine; the intoxicated group prayed and garbled the opening of Sūrat al-Kāfirūn, after which the verse was revealed.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p88/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · علي بن أبي طالب | reports | A second version says ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf was the person they put forward to lead prayer and who mixed up the sūra.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p88/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | reports | The phrase is interpreted either as not exposing oneself to intoxication at prayer times or as not entering prayer while intoxicated; the author prefers the first because an intoxicated person cannot understand what is addressed to him.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p88/r4] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الجمهور | reports | Most exegetes say the intoxication is from wine.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p88/r5] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الضحاك | reports | Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says the intoxication is from sleep; the author considers this far-fetched.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p88/r6] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | This verse temporarily allowed drinking outside prayer times, then the later prohibition of wine abrogated that allowance.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p90/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن قتيبة | reports | Ibn Qutayba says junub derives from distance or separation.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p90/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjāj notes that junub has the same form for one man, two men, and a group, as raḍī does.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p90/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | reports | One explanation for the term is that semen has moved away from its proper place.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p90/r4] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | reports | Another explanation is that a person in this state must avoid prayer, Qurʾān recitation, touching the muṣḥaf, and entering a mosque.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p90/r5] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · علي، مجاهد، الحكم، قتادة، ابن زيد، مقاتل، الفراء، الزجاج | reports | One interpretation permits a traveler without water to perform tayammum and pray while junub; on this view, passing by means being a traveler and approaching prayer means performing it.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p90/r6] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن مسعود، أنس بن مالك، الحسن، سعيد بن المسيب، عكرمة، عطاء الخراساني، الزهري، عمرو بن دينار، أبو الضحى، أحمد، الشافعي، ابن قتيبة | reports | Another interpretation bars a junub person from entering or sitting in mosques except to pass through; Ibn ʿAbbās and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr are reported with both views.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p91#2/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | The “or” functions like “and”; otherwise the sick and traveler would owe purification even without the occurrence of ritual impurity.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p91#2/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن قتيبة | reports | Al-Ghāʾiṭ literally means low, level ground; the place is used euphemistically for the act of excretion, like other container or vehicle terms used for their contents.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p91#2/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | The author gives parallels: rāwiya is properly the camel carrying water, and ẓaʿāʾin are properly the howdahs carrying women; ʿadhira likewise names excretion from the courtyards where it was left.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p91#2/r4] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن كثير، نافع، أبو عمرو، عاصم، ابن عامر | reports | Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr, ʿĀṣim, and Ibn ʿĀmir read lāmastum with an alif here and in al-Māʾida. | mentions 5:6
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p91#2/r5] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · حمزة، الكسائي، خلف، المفضل عن عاصم، الوليد بن عتبة عن ابن عامر | reports | Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, Khalaf, and the cited transmitters from ʿĀṣim and Ibn ʿĀmir read lamastum without an alif here and in al-Māʾida. | mentions 5:6
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p91#2/r6] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · علي، ابن عباس، الحسن، مجاهد، قتادة | reports | One legal interpretation takes touching women to mean sexual intercourse.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p91#2/r7] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن مسعود، ابن عمر، الشعبي، عبيدة، عطاء، ابن سيرين، النخعي، النهدي، الحكم، حماد | reports | Another legal interpretation takes the phrase as touching a woman with the hand.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p91#2/r8] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · أبو علي | reports | Abū ʿAlī says touch can mean contact by hand but is extended to other kinds of contact; 72:8 uses “we touched the heaven” for attempting to reach its secrets. | mentions 72:8
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p91#2/r9] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · أبو علي | reports | The wording “they touched it with their hands” in 6:7 specifies hands to distinguish literal touching from the extended sense; likewise “sons from your loins” in 4:23 distinguishes biological sons from merely named sons. | mentions 6:7, 4:23
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p91/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · مجاهد | reports | Mujāhid says the verse came down after a sick Anṣārī man unable to rise for ablution and without a servant asked the Prophet for help.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p91/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · إبراهيم النخعي | reports | Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī says the verse came down after the Prophet's companions suffered spreading wounds while becoming junub and brought their difficulty to him.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p91/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · القاضي أبو يعلى | holds | Qāḍī Abū Yaʿlā says illness allows tayammum when using water would cause harm, whether or not death is feared; travel allows it with no water on short or long journeys. [IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p93/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · عائشة | reports | The Prophet and ʿĀʾisha were traveling without water when her necklace was lost; the search delayed them, and the tayammum verse was revealed. [IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p93/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · عائشة | reports | A second account says ʿĀʾisha borrowed a necklace from Asmāʾ and lost it; the Prophet sent men to search, and when prayer came without water they prayed without ablution and reported it, whereupon the tayammum verse was revealed. [IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p93/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | Tayammum means to intend or aim; the author says he discussed this earlier under “do not aim at the bad.” | mentions 2:267
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p93/r4] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · علي، ابن مسعود، الفراء، أبو عبيد، الزجاج، ابن قتيبة | reports | These authorities say al-ṣaʿīd means soil.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p93/r5] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shāfiʿī says the name al-ṣaʿīd applies only to soil that has dust.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p93/r6] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | reports | Two interpretations of ṭayyib are pure and lawful.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p95/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | The part of the face wiped in tayammum is the same area delimited for washing in ablution.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p95/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · عمار عن النبي | reports | One view limits the hands to the wrists, citing the Prophet's report that tayammum is one strike for the face and palms; this is held by Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib, ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ, ʿIkrima, al-Awzāʿī, Makḥūl, Mālik, Aḥmad, Isḥāq, and Dāwūd.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p95/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن عباس عن النبي | reports | A second view extends wiping to the elbows, citing Ibn ʿAbbās's report that the Prophet wiped his forearms; it is held by Ibn ʿUmar, his son Sālim, al-Ḥasan, Abū Ḥanīfa, and al-Shāfiʿī, while al-Shaʿbī is reported with both views.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p95/r4] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · عمار بن ياسر، الزهري | reports | A third view extends wiping from the fingertips to the armpits, citing ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir's report of a travel concession and two strikes, one for the face and one to the shoulders and armpits; al-Zuhrī holds this view.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p96/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الخطابي | reports | Al-Khaṭṭābī says ʿafuww is an intensive form and means pardoning sins and leaving the wrongdoer unpunished.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p96/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | reports | Another explanation derives the word from wind erasing a trace: the pardoner wipes away sins through pardon.

[RAZI-FULL:v10p87#2/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The mosque reading answers that people ordinarily go to the mosque for prayer, so whatever prevents prayer also counts as a reason not to go to the mosque.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p87/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | One occasion report says ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf served food and drink to companions while wine was still permitted; after drinking, an imam garbled the recitation at Maghrib, prompting the verse. [RAZI-FULL:v10p87/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · عمر | reports | When ʿUmar heard the ruling, he prayed that God issue a command about wine because it harms minds and property; the revelation of al-Māʾida came the next morning. | mentions 5:90
[RAZI-FULL:v10p87/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās gives another occasion: before wine was forbidden, senior Companions drank and came to the mosque to pray with the Messenger, so God prohibited this.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p87/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · ابن عباس وابن مسعود والحسن والشافعي | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd, and al-Ḥasan take ‘prayer’ to mean the mosque, and al-Shāfiʿī adopts this view; it can mean ‘place of prayer’ by common ellipsis, as ṣalawāt means prayer sites at 22:40. | mentions 22:40
[RAZI-FULL:v10p87/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الأكثرون | reports | The majority take ṣalāt here to mean the prayer itself: do not perform it while intoxicated.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p88/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الواحدي | reports | Al-Wāḥidī says sukkārā is the plural of sakrān; adjectives on faʿlān take the plural patterns fuʿālā and fuʿālā, as in kasālā.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p88/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The root sense of sakr is blocking a path: it describes stopping a water channel, a confused eye, or water diverted from its course; wine blocks reason from penetrating as it does in sobriety. [RAZI-FULL:v10p88/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · جمهور الصحابة والتابعين | reports | The majority of Companions and Successors understand the word as intoxication from wine, the opposite of sobriety.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p88/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الضحاك | reports | Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says the word means sleep rather than wine intoxication: sleep blocks the channels of the spirit, preventing sight and hearing from reaching the body’s exterior.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p88/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الفرزدق | reports | Al-Farazdaq’s line compares sleep to wine, supporting the use of sakr for sleep.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p88/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Al-Ḍaḥḥāk argues that the verse describes sleep because an unaware person cannot be charged with a duty; the Prophet’s report lifts the pen from children, the insane, and sleepers until they wake or recover.

[RAZI-FULL:v10p90/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · ابن مسعود وابن عمر والشعبي والنخعي والشافعي | reports | Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿUmar, al-Shaʿbī, al-Nakhaʿī, and al-Shāfiʿī understand the phrase as skin contact, with or without intercourse.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p90/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | prefers | Al-Rāzī prefers skin contact: lams literally means touching by hand, while restricting it to intercourse is figurative; mulāmasa also does not literally mean intercourse, so the two canonical readings should retain compatible literal senses.

[RAZI-FULL:v10p90/r9] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أنصار قول الجماع | reports | They also argue that ‘coming from the place of need’ already covers minor impurity; if touching women also meant minor impurity, the verse would omit major impurity, so it must mean intercourse.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p91/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | Rāzī rejects the preceding interpretations as unsupported departures from the wording; reading this part as janāba would repeat the ruling already stated.

item.text: The later sources add detailed legal differences about water access, illness, the materials used for tayammum, and how far to wipe. I’m tracking those as distinct questions so the map can show what each ruling turns on.

[BAYDAWI-FULL:4:43-44/r1] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The Ḥanafīs allow striking hard stone, while al-Bayḍāwī’s school requires dust to adhere; min in the cited verse is partitive, and treating it as a starting point is strained.

[BAYDAWI-FULL:4:43/r1] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Do not enter prayer while intoxicated through sleep or wine until sober and understanding what you say in prayer.

[BAYDAWI-FULL:4:43/r11] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The phrase marks the end of the prohibition for a junub person; it also teaches worshippers to avoid distractions and purify the soul.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:4:43/r12] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | The illness may make water use dangerous or prevent reaching it; in either case, the person is treated as lacking water.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:4:43/r13] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The traveler is excused when water is unavailable.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:4:43/r14] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Coming from the privy means becoming impure through discharge from either outlet; ghāʾiṭ originally means a low-lying place.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:4:43/r15] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The phrase may mean skin touching skin; al-Shāfiʿī uses it as evidence that touching women invalidates ablution.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:4:43/r16] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | Alternatively, the phrase means sexual intercourse; lamasa is less commonly used as a euphemism for intercourse than mulāmasa.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:4:43/r17] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · حمزة والكسائي | reports | Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read lāmastum here and in al-Māʾida.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:4:43/r18] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | “Finding no water” includes being unable to use it, since what one is barred from using counts as unavailable.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:4:43/r19] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The classification covers minor or major impurity, usually prompted by illness or travel; it names the junub case and details ordinary and incidental causes for the other.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:4:43/r2] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · عبد الرحمن بن عوف | reports | When wine was permitted, Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf hosted Companions who drank until drunk; at Maghrib, one led prayer and recited a mistaken line, prompting this verse.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:4:43/r20] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Tayammum means deliberately turning to clean earth; the Ḥanafīs allow hard stone, while al-Bayḍāwī’s school requires dust to adhere, reading “from it” partitively.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:4:43/r3] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | Alternatively, “prayer” means its locations, the mosques; the point is to forbid excessive drinking and drunkenness rather than a drunk person approaching prayer.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:4:43/r4] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | The form is read sukārā with fatḥa; another form may be a plural like halkā, a singular for an intoxicated people, or a collective adjective like ḥublā.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:4:43/r5] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Junuban coordinates with the circumstantial clause “while you are intoxicated”; janub applies to all genders and numbers like a verbal noun.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:4:43/r6] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | The exception attaches to “while junub,” exempting travel when water is unavailable and tayammum is used, as the following clause indicates.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:4:43/r7] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | Alternatively, the phrase describes junub people, meaning “other than those passing through.”
[BAYDAWI-FULL:4:43/r8] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The exception is evidence that tayammum does not remove the state of ritual impurity.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:4:43/r9] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · الشافعي | reports | If prayer means mosques, those passing through are allowed to cross while junub; al-Shāfiʿī holds this view.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p223#3/r1] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | reports | When wine was lawful, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf hosted Companions who drank; their imam garbled al-Kāfirūn at Maghrib, and the verse was revealed.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p223#3/r10] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Al-ghāʾiṭ literally means a low, sunken area where people went to relieve themselves, so it euphemistically denotes defecation.

[NASAFI-FULL:v1p223#3/r12] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Not finding water includes being unable to use it because it is absent, distant, inaccessible, or blocked by a snake, predator, or enemy.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p223#3/r13] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The dry-ablution command covers the sick, travelers, people with minor impurity, and those in major impurity; it applies when each lacks usable water for the relevant reason.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p223#3/r14] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · حمزة وعلى | reports | Hamza and al-Kisa'i read the form without the alif, lamastum.

[NASAFI-FULL:v1p223#3/r16] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Dry ablution is valid on bare rock even without dust if the person strikes it and wipes with it.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p223#3/r17] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The min in the corresponding phrase in 5:6 marks the starting point, not a partitive meaning. | mentions 5:6
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p223#3/r18] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Tayyib means pure.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p223#3/r19] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The preposition bāʾ in the wiping phrase is said to be extra.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p223#3/r2] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Do not approach prayer in a state of intoxication until you understand what you are reciting.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p223#3/r20] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | God is ʿafuww by granting concessions and ease, and ghafūr by pardoning error and shortcoming.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p223#3/r3] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The drunken person's mistaken recitation of words of disbelief is not apostasy: he was still addressed as a believer, and no separation or renewal of faith was ordered.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p223#3/r4] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The community agrees that a person who mistakenly utters a word of disbelief is not judged an unbeliever.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p223#3/r5] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Junuban is coordinated with the circumstantial phrase wa-antum sukārā, both being accusative states: do not pray drunk or in major impurity.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p223#3/r6] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Junub has the same form for singular and plural and for masculine and feminine because it functions like the verbal noun ijnāb.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p223#3/r7] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · أبو حنيفة | prefers | For a junub person, prayer means the prayer itself; a resident must wash, while a traveler without water may use dry ablution, which is the Hanafi reading also transmitted from Ali.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p223#3/r8] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · الشافعى | reports | Al-Shafiʿi takes prayer to mean mosques: a junub person may not enter one except to pass through when needed.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p223#3/r9] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The exception describes a junub traveler passing through, and the reference to travel reflects the usual lack of water on a journey.

[QASHANI:4:42-43/r15] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Lacking water means lacking knowledge that guides release from these states and purifies from them.

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p652/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الجمهور | reports | The majority say tayammum was revealed when the Companions lacked water on the al-Muraysīʿ expedition while searching for the necklace.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p652/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · النخعي | reports | Al-Nakhaʿī says the revelation concerned wounded people who became junub.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p652/r12] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | Another account says the occasion involved ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p652/r13] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · داود | reports | Dāwūd applies the general wording of illness without limits on severity or duration and allows tayammum to anyone who fits the name sick.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p652/r14] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · العلماء | reports | Other jurists restrict illness to conditions such as smallpox, measles, or dangerous ailments where water may harm; they agree tayammum is allowed when harm is feared.

 well-known Mālikī position and al-Muzanī require rubbing the body during ghusl; the majority say immersion or pouring water suffices without rubbing.

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p652/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو حنيفة وأصحابه | reports | The verse names washing without stating an intention requirement; Abū Ḥanīfa and his companions do not require intention for water purification.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p652/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · مالك والشافعي وأحمد وإسحاق وأبو ثور | reports | Mālik's well-known position, al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad, Isḥāq, and Abū Thawr require intention; al-Walīd ibn Muslim transmitted the contrary view from Mālik.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p653#2/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو حنيفة | reports | Abū Ḥanīfa reads the phrase as intercourse, not hand-touch; even a kiss with desire does not invalidate ablution in his school.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p653#2/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The shift to third person in جاء أحد delicately avoids directly attributing the toilet need to the addressees, while illness, travel, and touching are said directly.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p653#2/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Not finding water normally means searching without reaching it; for the sick, existing water that cannot be used counts legally as absent.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p653#2/r12] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The water-finding clause coordinates with the conditional verbs, and tayammum is the response; the command applies if any of four causes occurs with water absent.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p653#2/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · مالك وأحمد وإسحاق | reports | Mālik says intercourse requires tayammum and hand-touch does so only with pleasure; without desire there is no ablution. Aḥmad and Isḥāq agree on the desire distinction.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p653#2/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الشافعي وابن مسعود وابن عمر والزهري وربيعة وعبيدة والشعبي وإبراهيم ومنصور وابن سيرين | reports | Al-Shāfiʿī and the listed authorities hold that any bodily contact with a woman's body invalidates purity.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p653#2/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الأوزاعي | reports | Al-Awzāʿī says contact invalidates ablution when it is by hand, but not otherwise.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p653#2/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · حمزة والكسائي | reports | Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read لمستم without the long alif; the other six of the seven canonical readers use the long alif.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p653#2/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The long-alif form can correspond to the simple verb, like جاوزت الشيء وجزته; its form does not distinguish active from passive though the meaning can, and al-Shāfiʿī applies it to both toucher and touched in his stronger view.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p653#2/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | أو على سفر is accusative by coordination with مرضى.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p653#2/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The past verbs جاء and لامستم can be predicates after كان without an implied قد; ellipsis is strained because they coordinate with the predicate.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p653#2/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The pronoun in فلم تجدوا refers to those named in all four conditions, with a shift between direct address and the third-person أحد.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p653/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو حنيفة ومالك | reports | Abū Ḥanīfa and Mālik permit tayammum when one fears illness will begin or worsen, or recovery will be delayed.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p653/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الجمهور | reports | If water is too scarce to use without risking thirst, the majority permit tayammum.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p653/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الفقهاء | reports | There is no disagreement that a person who finds water at its ordinary price must buy it.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p653/r12] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو حنيفة والشافعي | reports | For water priced above its ordinary value, Abū Ḥanīfa and al-Shāfiʿī allow tayammum, whereas Mālik requires buying it with all one's wealth.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p653/r13] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Being blocked from water by an enemy, predator, or other obstacle is treated like lacking water.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p653/r14] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Coming from the toilet euphemizes the bodily event and extends to wind, urine, semen, and pre-ejaculatory fluid; these six events all invalidate ablution.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p653/r15] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن مسعود | reports | Ibn Masʿūd read من الغيط; it may be a verbal noun from غاط يغيط or originally a فيعل form with deletion like ميت.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p653/r16] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · عمرو بن مسعود وغيرهما | reports | ʿAmr ibn Masʿūd and others read the phrase as touching by hand; on this view a junub must wash or leave prayer until water is found.

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p653/r18] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · علي وابن عباس والحسن ومجاهد وقتادة | reports | ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, and Qatāda interpret the phrase as intercourse, in which case a junub may use tayammum.

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p653/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الليث والشافعي | reports | Al-Layth and another report from al-Shāfiʿī allow tayammum and prayer when time would expire, but require repeating after water is found.

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p655/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · عمار | reports | A Muslim report from ʿAmmār has the Prophet say one strike on the ground, blowing off dust, then wiping the face and palms suffices.

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p655/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو حنيفة والشافعي والثوري والليث وابن أبي سلمة | reports | Abū Ḥanīfa, al-Shāfiʿī, al-Thawrī, al-Layth, and others require wiping to the elbows; this is also attributed to Jābir, Ibn ʿUmar, al-Ḥasan, and Ibrāhīm.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p655/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · علي وعطاء والشعبي ومكحول والأوزاعي وأحمد وإسحاق وداود والطبري والشافعي | reports | Another group wipes only to the wrists; this is reported from Mālik and was al-Shāfiʿī's earlier position.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p656/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · عطاء والشعبي والأوزاعي وأحمد وإسحاق وداود والطبري | reports | The apparent verse and sound reports indicate one strike for face and hands; this is held by ʿAṭāʾ, one report from al-Shaʿbī, al-Awzāʿī's best-known report, Aḥmad, Isḥāq, Dāwūd, and al-Ṭabarī.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p656/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · مالك وأبو حنيفة والشافعي والثوري والليث وابن أبي سلمة | reports | Mālik in al-Mudawwana, Abū Ḥanīfa, al-Shāfiʿī, al-Thawrī, al-Layth, and Ibn Abī Salama require two strikes, one for face and one for hands.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p656/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن أبي ليلى والحسن | reports | Ibn Abī Laylā and al-Ḥasan also require two strikes, each wiping face, arms, and elbows; Abū Ḥayyān says no other scholar held this.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p656/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Many tayammum rulings are treated in law books and al-Māʾida; its qualification is applied to this verse and supports al-Shāfiʿī's requirement that some material be transferred to the face and hands.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p656/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhsharī asks how the al-Māʾida phrase فامسحوا بوجوهكم وأيديكم منه can require part of the earth when bare rock has no soil, and answers that من marks a starting point.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p656/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | Abū Ḥayyān calls the starting-point reading strained: Arabs understand مسحت برأسه من الدهن والماء والتراب as partitive, and he approves yielding to truth over disputation.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p656/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhsharī takes the divine description as an allusion to legal concession and ease: God forgives and pardons, so He chooses ease over hardship.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p656/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | Abū Ḥayyān criticizes al-Zamakhsharī for accepting the apparent sense here despite usually distorting wording for his school, and for speaking of forgiveness without the repentance qualification he usually requires.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:43#2/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The cited line continues with the question of how a youth intoxicated by both love and wine could recover.

[SAMIN-DURR:4:43#2/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The root’s general meaning is obstruction: it describes sleep clouding a hawk’s eye and a river ceasing to flow.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:43#2/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | حتى is a preposition meaning إلى, attached to the prohibitive verb; the following verb is subjunctive with أن understood.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:43#2/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | ما can be relative or an indefinite noun qualified by a clause, with an omitted resumptive pronoun on either analysis, or a verbal noun particle; omission on the last analysis is only required by Ibn al-Sarraj and his followers.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:43#3/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | جنبا is accusative as a circumstantial element coordinated with the preceding circumstantial clause; a single term coordinates with the sentence because it carries its meaning.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:43#3/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Repeating لا marks a separate prohibition for each state; prohibition under both states together is still stronger and more fitting.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:43#3/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | جنب derives from جنابة, ‘distance’; a person is so called either for being distant from purity or for lying beside and touching another.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:43#3/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The cited verse uses جنابة in the sense relevant to the term جنب.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:43#3/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhshari explains that جنب has one form for singular, dual, plural, masculine, and feminine because it behaves like the verbal noun الإجناب.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:43#3/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Some Arabs also inflect جنب: dual جنبان, sound plural جنبون, and broken plural أجناب, like شلل.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:43#4/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | One parse makes عابري a circumstantial exception governed by the prohibition: do not approach in janāba except while traveling or crossing a mosque, depending on the interpretation.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:43#4/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhshari takes the exception as a circumstantial phrase from the addressees generally, with travel as an additional excuse and crossing the path as its expression.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:43#4/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · غير مسمى | reports | Alternatively, عابري describes جنبا, with إلا meaning غير: the prohibition concerns resident, unexcused people in janāba; this is clear if عبور means travel.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:43#4/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | If الصلاة means its locations, the phrase permits people in janāba to pass through mosques, because there is no other passage, or for another reason according to the disagree
